name: The soul as Essence, not as the form of the body
plain_explanation: Aristotle had argued the soul is simply the 'form' or organizing pattern of a living body, the way the shape of a statue is the form of its bronze. Plotinus rejects this, arguing that if the soul were merely the form of a material body, it could not perform the kind of pure intellectual activity it clearly does perform; instead the soul is an eternal, immaterial reality (Essence) only temporarily associated with a body through desire.
precise_definition: Plotinus's argument, developed in the Fourth Ennead (Seventh Tractate), that the soul cannot be identical either to matter (as the Stoics held) or to the form of a material body (as Aristotle, unnamed, held), because the soul's unity and its capacity for intellectual activity would then be impossible; instead the soul belongs to the eternal order of Essence, and is therefore immortal.
why_it_mattered: This is presented by Russell as a genuine philosophical improvement in clarity over both Plato and Aristotle's treatments of the soul-body relationship, and as the fullest ancient statement of an argument only implicit in Plato's own reasoning that the soul is immortal because the Forms/ideas it grasps are themselves eternal.
historical_origin: Developed in the Fourth Ennead, Seventh Tractate, 'On Immortality.'
examples: Plotinus's argument against Stoic materialism: since the soul is a unity, and matter (being passive) cannot have created itself or preceded soul, the soul cannot itself be material
The soul entering the body through 'appetite' -- likened by Russell to a composer who first imagines music internally, then wishes to hear it externally performed
competing_positions: Aristotle's view that the soul is the form of the body (rejected)
influence_on_later_thinkers: Influences later Christian and medieval doctrines of an immaterial, immortal soul distinct from bodily form.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Underpins Plotinus's account of reincarnation and moral punishment after death.
